exam: A patient with severe malaria develops rapid breathing and a lactate of 12 mmol/L — what immediate steps do you take? — Assess airway, give oxygen, start IV fluids, check for shock, give IV thiamine, treat malaria.
How do you differentiate Type A from Type B lactic acidosis at the bedside? — Look for hypoxia/shock (Type A) versus drug/toxin exposure, liver disease, thiamine deficiency (Type B).

Why is giving large volumes of normal saline potentially harmful in a patient with cardiac failure and lactic acidosis? — It can worsen pulmonary oedema, impair tissue perfusion, and dilute bicarbonate.

A patient on metformin presents with vomiting and a lactate of 8 mmol/L — what is the next management decision? — Hold metformin, assess renal function, give IV fluids, consider renal replacement if lactate rises.
What laboratory result would make you suspect a mixed high‑anion‑gap acidosis? — Elevated lactate plus a low bicarbonate with a normal or low serum ketone level.
Explain why a patient with severe anemia can develop lactic acidosis even with normal blood pressure. — Reduced oxygen‑carrying capacity forces tissues into anaerobic metabolism, producing lactate.
When is renal replacement therapy indicated for lactic acidosis? — Lactate >20 mmol/L, refractory acidosis (pH <7.1) despite fluids, or concurrent renal failure.
What is the significance of a normal anion gap in a patient with metabolic acidosis? — Suggests a hyperchloraemic (non‑anion‑gap) acidosis; lactic acidosis would be unlikely.
ai.title: Lactic Acidosis
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Lactic acidosis is a high anion‑gap metabolic acidosis caused by excess lactate production or impaired clearance. Recognise common tropical causes, assess severity, and act quickly to treat the underlying problem and support organ function.

sections.p: Lactate is produced during anaerobic glycolysis. When production exceeds hepatic/renal clearance, serum lactate rises >5 mmol/L and pH falls <7.35, defining lactic acidosis. It can be life‑threatening and often signals tissue hypoxia or severe metabolic disturbance.

b: Type A: shock, severe anemia, cardiac failure, severe malaria, severe pneumonia, sepsis
Type B: liver failure, renal failure, thiamine deficiency, drugs (metformin, antiretrovirals), malignancy, toxins
Severity: mild (5‑10 mmol/L), moderate (10‑20 mmol/L), severe (>20 mmol/L) with rising mortality
sections.p: Distinguish Type A (hypoxic) from Type B (non‑hypoxic) mechanisms, stage severity, and identify reversible causes common in low‑resource settings.

b: Look for shock signs: cold extremities, delayed capillary refill, low MAP
Check for underlying infections: malaria, TB, HIV‑related sepsis
Consider drug history: metformin, antiretrovirals, herbal remedies
sections.p: Patients present with rapid breathing, confusion, hypotension, and a fruity or sour smell on breath. In low‑resource hospitals, the diagnosis often relies on bedside clues and limited labs.

t.b: Confirms metabolic acidosis and calculates anion gap; low HCO3‑ and pH <7.35 indicate severity
Quantifies lactate; >5 mmol/L confirms lactic acidosis, trends guide response
Shows electrolytes, renal function, and helps calculate anion gap; if unavailable, use bedside urine dipstick for ketones to rule out ketoacidosis

t.a: Full blood count and malaria smear
t.b: Detects severe anemia or malaria, common Type A triggers in East Africa
Identifies deficiency, especially in chronic alcoholics or malnourished patients

b: Restore tissue oxygenation: give oxygen, treat shock with fluids (crystalloids) and, if needed, vasopressors (e.g., norepinephrine) once volume‑responsive
Stop offending drugs: hold metformin, antiretrovirals, or toxic herbal preparations
Consider renal replacement therapy if lactate >20 mmol/L with renal failure and no response to fluids
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then provide supportive care to improve perfusion and clear lactate.

b: Identify Type A vs. Type B by asking about hypoxia, shock, drug exposure, liver disease
Know the anion‑gap calculation and cut‑offs
Explain why giving bicarbonate alone can worsen intracellular acidosis
sections.p: Examiners test your ability to recognise, differentiate, and act quickly.

b: Assuming all high‑anion‑gap acidosis is ketoacidosis; always check lactate
Delaying thiamine in malnourished patients; can precipitate Wernicke’s encephalopathy
Giving large fluid boluses in patients with severe cardiac failure without monitoring
sections.p: Pitfalls often arise from missing reversible causes or over‑relying on limited labs.

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden drop in MAP <65 mmHg despite fluids
Lactate >20 mmol/L with worsening mental status
